label: Claude Fable 5.2
output:
Peter, I'm replying to you, but mostly so Brenda has this before the 18th, since she asked whether anyone has actually closed the window. We did.

I'm HR manager at a logistics company with about 340 staff across a Nairobi depot and a Mombasa one. They are mostly drivers, turn-boys, loaders and warehouse clerks, so the pay profile is similar to Brenda's line workers.

First, where I agree with you. An informal scheme where someone comes to the HR office, explains themselves and gets a yes or no is a bad scheme. That's what we had, and it's what Brenda has now: no limit, no rules, and HR as the lender of first resort, exactly as you describe. Nine years of running payroll also means you've seen the leavers who owe and the reconciliations from the inside, which most of us in HR haven't. Our Finance team made your argument in early 2025 almost word for word, and I couldn't answer it then any better than Brenda can now.

So we did what you're recommending. We gave two months' notice rather than your three, ran one financial literacy session with the SACCO, and closed advances in February 2025.

You said people adjust after a cycle or two. Ours adjusted too, by going to the loan apps. Before we closed, reception got a handful of calls from debt collectors and loan apps. In the six months after, they logged 61. Some of the apps were calling supervisors who had been listed as "referees", so supervisors were fielding collection calls about their own team members in the middle of a shift.

Unplanned absence on the two days after month-end went up. Our fleet manager linked at least three missed Mombasa runs to drivers who were off "sorting out" loans.

The case I remember best is a loader at the Mombasa depot. By the time he came to me he had six apps running at once and was borrowing from one to pay another. It took payroll and me four months to unwind it with him.

That's why I can't agree that the apps are the employee's own decision and their own contract. On paper they are. In practice the collection lands at the workplace, on our supervisors' phones and on our delivery schedule.

On the SACCO, ours is good, but a loan takes two to three weeks to process and needs guarantors. That is useless for a child sent home over school fees on a Tuesday. The literacy session was worth doing and I'd do it again, but someone on KES 28,000 a month has very little room to build an emergency fund, however well they budget.

We reopened in September 2025, this time as a written policy:

- Maximum 40% of net pay.
- One advance per pay cycle.
- Repaid in full at the next payroll, so nothing rolls over.
- No fee.
- Requests go through the payroll portal, not my office.
- Before approving, payroll checks the Employment Act limit of two-thirds of wages on total deductions, so nobody ends up with nothing at month end.

Since then we get about 55 to 70 requests a month, averaging around KES 9,000. We have recovered everything except from two leavers, and the total written off for the year is roughly KES 14,000. That is against something like six or seven million shillings advanced over the year. Your point about leavers is fair, it does happen, but with a cap and one-cycle repayment the loss is small.

On your two other concerns:

- **HR time:** you were right about the old scheme. Under the new one I don't approve anything. It's a rules check in payroll, and nobody has to sit in my office explaining their private business.
- **Living on next month's money:** some people will use it often, and I won't pretend otherwise. But the worst case is 40% of one month, at no cost, cleared every payroll. The alternative we saw was six apps with interest, calling the supervisor.

Our Finance Manager now defends the scheme himself. His objection was the same as Brenda's Finance Manager's: it messes up the forecast. What changed his mind was that the impact is now known in advance. It's a fixed ceiling he can plan around, not a surprise.

Brenda, for the 18th, I'd bring three things.

1. **Your own advance numbers for the last 12 months.** Payroll will have them: how many advances a month, the average amount, how many people take one every month, and how much you've actually failed to recover. I suspect the write-off figure is smaller than Finance assumes.

2. **The costs of closing that Finance won't see.** Advances sit in one place where Finance can count them. For us, the costs of closing were spread across departments:
   - fleet took the missed runs;
   - supervisors and reception took the calls;
   - payroll and HR took the months of unwinding.

   None of it appeared on a single budget line, so on paper closing looked free. Ask them to weigh the administration and write-offs against that, and use our figures as an example if it helps.

3. **A written policy for the MD to say yes to.** Don't defend the current arrangement, because it's indefensible, and saying so yourself will help you with Finance. Propose a replacement with:
   - a cap as a percentage of net pay;
   - a frequency limit;
   - full repayment at the next payroll;
   - an approval route through payroll instead of your office;
   - the two-thirds deduction check.

   Your Finance Manager can then work out the maximum exposure in any month before he agrees to anything. Kiprono said the same above: Finance stopped complaining once they could see a ceiling.

Peter, I don't think you're wrong about what an unmanaged scheme does. I just think the answer is rules and limits. We tried closing the window, and it cost us more than the advances ever did.

Brenda, if you want more detail on how the portal request and the deduction check work, ask here and I'll explain what I can.

---

I described the depots as Nairobi and Mombasa instead of naming Embakasi and Changamwe, since the two locations plus the headcount could identify the firm. The "six or seven million shillings advanced" figure is my own estimate from your monthly requests and average, so check it against payroll or cut it.

reasons: The closing note addresses the user about writing choices rather than continuing the board reply.
